title: Diabetic ketoacidosis in adults
instruction: Look at Texts A–D. Questions 1–7: which text? Questions 8–15: word/short phrase from the texts. Questions 16–20: complete the sentence. Spelling matters. Target: 15 minutes.
sharedWhichPrompt: In which text can you find information about

texts.label: A
texts.heading: Diagnostic criteria and severity classification
texts.body:
Diagnostic triad
A diagnosis of DKA requires all three of the following:
• Blood glucose >11 mmol/L (or a confirmed diagnosis of diabetes mellitus)
• Blood ketones ≥3.0 mmol/L, or urine ketones 2+ or above on dipstick
• Bicarbonate <15 mmol/L and/or venous pH <7.3

Severity classification
Mild: venous pH 7.25–7.29; bicarbonate 15–17.9 mmol/L; patient alert and orientated.
Moderate: venous pH 7.0–7.24; bicarbonate <15 mmol/L.
Severe — any one of the following: venous pH <7.0; bicarbonate <5 mmol/L; Glasgow Coma Scale <12; SpO₂ <92% on air; systolic BP <90 mmHg; heart rate >100 or <60 bpm; anion gap >16 mmol/L.

Anion gap
Calculated as Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); normal range 12 ± 2 mmol/L. A raised anion gap alongside ketonaemia confirms a high anion gap metabolic acidosis typical of DKA.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Fixed-rate insulin infusion and fluid regimen
texts.body:
Fixed-rate insulin infusion (FRII)
Prescribe 0.1 units/kg/hour of soluble insulin made up in 0.9% sodium chloride. Do not stop or reduce the patient's usual background (basal) insulin while FRII is running.

Monitoring and dose adjustment
Check blood ketones and capillary glucose hourly. The target is a blood ketone fall of ≥0.5 mmol/L per hour. If ketones are not falling at this rate, increase the infusion rate by 1 unit/hour. Do not use a variable-rate insulin infusion (sliding scale) in DKA.

Glucose management
When blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, add 10% glucose at 125 mL/hour alongside continuing 0.9% sodium chloride. Maintain blood glucose at 14–17 mmol/L until ketones have cleared.

Fluid replacement
Give 1 litre of 0.9% NaCl over the first hour, then reassess haemodynamic status and adjust subsequent bags accordingly.

texts.label: C
texts.heading: Potassium replacement guide
texts.body:
Hypokalaemia is the most dangerous electrolyte complication of DKA treatment. Check serum potassium before starting the fixed-rate insulin infusion and do not commence FRII if K⁺ is below 3.5 mmol/L.

Replacement guide (per litre of IV fluid)
• K⁺ >5.5 mmol/L: do not add potassium to IV fluids; recheck after 1 hour
• K⁺ 3.5–5.5 mmol/L: add 40 mmol potassium chloride (KCl) per litre of IV fluid
• K⁺ <3.5 mmol/L: do not start insulin; seek urgent senior or critical care review; replace potassium more aggressively before proceeding

Monitoring frequency
In severe or moderate DKA: check serum potassium every hour for the first 4 hours, then every 2 hours thereafter. In mild DKA: check every 2 hours.

Caution
Never add more than 40 mmol KCl to a single 1-litre bag without senior authorisation. Hyperkalaemia (K⁺ >5.5 mmol/L) may worsen transiently as acidosis is corrected.

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Resolution criteria, subcutaneous insulin transition and precipitant review
texts.body:
Resolution of DKA — all three criteria must be met
• Blood ketones <0.3 mmol/L
• Venous pH >7.3
• Bicarbonate >18 mmol/L
Blood glucose level alone is not a reliable marker of DKA resolution and must never be used as the sole criterion for stopping IV insulin.

Transition to subcutaneous insulin
Ensure the patient is eating and drinking normally before switching. Administer the patient's usual subcutaneous insulin dose, then wait 30–60 minutes before stopping the IV insulin infusion to prevent rebound ketosis. If the patient is newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, seek endocrinology advice before prescribing a subcutaneous regimen.

Precipitant review
Infection is the most common precipitant; send urine, blood cultures and a chest radiograph. Other precipitants include missed or insufficient insulin, new-onset type 1 diabetes, corticosteroids, antipsychotic drugs, and SGLT2 inhibitors (which can cause euglycaemic DKA even with near-normal glucose). Document the identified precipitant clearly in the discharge summary.
